newsitem.title: UK: Britain's OFT slams pensions industry.
newsitem.headline: Britain's OFT slams pensions industry.

text.p: Many people are losing out because of deficiencies in existing occupational and personal pension products, according to a report from Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) published on Tuesday.
The report criticises many personal pension plans for providing poor value with benefits frequently being eroded by the high cost of marketing and fund management.
While occupational pensions may have improved in recent years, it says those who leave early - as the majority do - lose out.
Director General of Fair Trading John Bridgeman called for radical changes in attitude and provision if consumer interests were to be adequately safeguarded by Britain's pensions industry.
And he called on government ministers to incorporate passively-managed products in future pensions policy.
"I am recommending a genuinely portable, passively managed 'defined contribution' scheme. It would need to be adequately funded, where appropriate, by the employer," said Bridgeman.
"It would not penalise those who change jobs and would not have to bear heavy fund management and distribution costs."
The OFT blueprint -- the designated personal pension -- would employ a tracker fund and would provide more flexible pension arrangements.
Wide provision should be encouraged by changes to the tax system, said Bridgeman.

The OFT report found that existing personal pension plan expenses were often loaded onto the early years of the plan and bore disproportionately on those discontinuing the pension. Employers' contributions were often inadequate or non-existent.
Employees who moved employers several times could find his occupational pension up to 30 percent lower that someone who stayed in the same scheme.
In addition, the pension rights that employees received on leaving "defined benefit" schemes were subject to a large degree of actuarial discretion which could dramatically reduce their size.
Problems with defined contribution schemes arose from inefficient and expensive selling methods and costly fund management.
Products were marketed in an unnecessarily complex way by emphasising superior investment performance which Bridgeman described as "insubstantial and illusory".
"There is no convincing evidence that fund managers can consistently outperform the market over the period of a pension plan although the industry does not like to face up to this," said Bridgeman.
